# Measures of Central Tendency {#sec-central-tendency}

Measures of central tendency describe the typical or central value in a data set.
In AS91946, you should choose the centre measure that best matches the shape of
the data and the context of the question.

## Why centre matters

When you compare groups or interpret a distribution, centre tells you where most
values sit. A good statistical description usually includes both:

- centre (what is typical), and
- spread (how variable values are).

## Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Mean | Sum of values divided by the number of values |
| Median | Middle value of ordered data |
| Mode | Most frequent value |

## Core formulas

$$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}$$

For an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle
ordered values.

## Worked example

Data: $[12, 14, 16, 17, 18, 21, 24, 60]$

1. Mean

$$\bar{x} = \frac{12+14+16+17+18+21+24+60}{8} = \frac{182}{8} = 22.75$$

2. Median

Ordered middle two values are $17$ and $18$, so:

$$\text{Median} = \frac{17+18}{2} = 17.5$$

3. Mode

No repeated values, so this data set has no mode.

Interpretation: the high value $60$ pulls the mean upward, so the median gives a
better description of the typical value.

## Choosing the right measure

| Situation | Better centre measure | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Roughly symmetric distribution, no outliers | Mean | Uses all values |
| Skewed distribution or outliers present | Median | Resistant to extreme values |
| Categorical data or most common value needed | Mode | Identifies most frequent category/value |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exam language frame
"The median is a better measure of centre here because the distribution is
right-skewed and includes high outliers, which would pull the mean upward."
:::

## Quick R check (optional)

```{r}
example_data <- c(12, 14, 16, 17, 18, 21, 24, 60)

cat("Mean:", mean(example_data), "\n")
cat("Median:", median(example_data), "\n")
cat("Mode: none (all values unique)", "\n")
```

## Practice questions

1. Find the mean and median of $[7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]$.
2. Find the mean and median of $[5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 30]$.
3. For question 2, explain which measure of centre is more appropriate and why.

::: {.callout-note .content-visible collapse="true" when-format="html"}
## Answers
1. Mean $= 65/7 \approx 9.29$, median $= 9$.
2. Mean $= 65/6 \approx 10.83$, median $= (7+8)/2 = 7.5$.
3. Median is more appropriate because the outlier $30$ inflates the mean.
:::
